prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of magic-angle flat bands and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I keep B016 as my final position. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model of 2011 is a compact, quantitative electronic-structure prediction: two rotated graphene layers, an interlayer tunnelling term and a moire superlattice give nearly flat bands at a magic angle. Jarillo-Herrero's group then found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle in 2018, so the experiment tested exactly the object the theory described. Many independent groups have reproduced the insulating states and the superconducting domes, and the same logic has been carried to twisted multilayers and moire transition-metal dichalcogenides, where band width and filling are tunable. As a materials theorist I regard this as a direct demonstration that the band structure of a real material can be engineered so that correlations dominate. The citation I propose is limited to the prediction of the flat bands and the discovery of the correlated insulating and superconducting states. It says nothing about the pairing mechanism, which answers the chair's question on that point. Round 1 did not change my reading of the science. What it changed is how I weigh the competing configurations. B048 has a larger bloc, but its attribution problem is structural, whereas the B016 problem is the routine one of co-first authors.
statement.case_against: The field is about seven years past the 2018 experiments, the superconducting pairing mechanism is open, and the nature of some correlated states is still argued. The prize would therefore rest on the existence of the phenomena and on the platform, not on a settled microscopic explanation. Attribution is also imperfect. Yuan Cao and the other first authors of the 2018 papers, Dean and collaborators on moire heterostructures, and earlier continuum-model work by Santos, Peres and Castro Neto fall outside the three names. If the committee thinks maturity should decide this year, B048 or B049 has more years of confirmation and I would not call that an unreasonable view.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B041 to B048 and says the citation can be anchored on the Z2 state and its first observation. He also notes that B016 is the cleaner theory-plus-experiment triple if the attribution of B048 cannot be handled within three names.
responses.response: We agree on the diagnostic: if the attribution cannot be resolved, B016 is cleaner, and I think it cannot be resolved here. The HgTe experiment tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and Kane and Mele's graphene model was not the realised material. A citation limited to the Z2 state and its first observation would be accurate, but it would name two theorists whose model was not what Molenkamp measured and omit the step that told him where to look. For B016 the model that was predicted is the system that was measured. Your question about the 2016 overlap is fair, and I agree it is smaller than Pearce and Lindroth fear, since Z2 matter without a magnetic field is distinct from the 2016 work. That does not remove the attribution cost, so I stay with B016.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B048 first for its two decades of confirmation and a natural theory-plus-experiment triple, and asks whether the committee should rather wait for the pairing mechanism in twisted graphene to be understood.
responses.response: I do not dispute that B048 is the more mature discovery. I disagree that the triple is natural. You concede that the BHZ proposal is a real gap that three names cannot close, and a prize committee has to write a citation it can defend. On maturity I would not wait for the mechanism. Nobel recognition has often gone to a discovery whose explanation was incomplete, and here the correlated insulators and the superconducting domes are the discovery, reproduced across many laboratories. The mechanism is a separate question and the citation will say nothing about it. I accept that seven years is short, which is why I treat B048 as a serious alternative and not a lesser one.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B048 for the clean boundaries of the discovery and wants the three names justified on the record, not because they form a tidy trio. She would rather face the BHZ omission openly than add a fourth name.
responses.response: I agree that the names must be justified on the record and I apply the same test to B016. My justification is Bistritzer and MacDonald for the prediction, and Jarillo-Herrero as the leader of the group that made the discovery. I accept that Cao and the co-first authors are a real omission, and I do not claim the three-person limit treats them fairly. The difference is that there the omitted people belong to the same experimental team as a credited name, so a citation worded around the discovery by that group is accurate. For B048 the omitted step lies between the two credited halves. I also note that you put B016 second, so on this point I think we differ in weight and not in principle.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps B049 first for a new regime of many-atom interrogation and a clean two-name credit, and is troubled by timing for B016 and the possible read of lattice clocks as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: On the physics I accept your argument that the magic-wavelength condition is an insight and not just engineering, and that two named people with a proposal-plus-realisation split is the cleanest credit on the list. I am not an atomic physicist and I cannot weigh Katori's priority over other early lattice-clock proposers, which you and Kroll both say rests on recollection. That uncertainty, plus the pending redefinition of the second, is why I keep B049 as an alternative and not as my choice. I would not call it a weaker case than B016. If the committee decides that maturity and credit cleanliness outweigh the breadth of support, B049 is where I would move before B048.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, prefers B016 and gives the seven-year timing more weight than the chair summary's question suggests; he lists B048 and B049 as alternatives.
responses.response: We agree on the science, and I have the same two reservations, the open mechanism and the co-first-author problem. I do not share your concern about timing as a reason to wait, but I would hold the citation to the prediction and the discovery of the states, as the chair's question suggests, and drop the broader field wording I used in round 1, since 'opening the field of moire quantum materials' praises a field and not a discovery. I also agree that breadth of opening support is not a substitute for scientific judgment. I use it only to note that B016 was ranked by seven members and nobody argued against it on science.

uncertainties: Whether seven years of confirmation, with the pairing mechanism unsettled, is enough for the committee, or whether a more mature configuration should come first this year.

Whether a citation limited to the prediction of flat bands and the discovery of the correlated states is accurate enough about the role of Yuan Cao and the other first authors of the 2018 experiments.
Whether the committee regards the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap in B048 as repairable by wording, in which case I would reconsider B048 as my second choice.
My view of B049 relies on a limited knowledge of atomic physics, and I cannot independently assess the priority among early lattice-clock proposers.
statement.conflict_note: I have no personal or institutional connection to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer in my profile, and no conflict for B048 or B049. I withdraw B006 from my alternatives. Its closeness to my own field of DFT and DFT+DMFT in Uppsala was the only disclosure I made in round 1, and it is no longer relevant to my configuration. My work in electronic-structure theory is professionally near twisted-bilayer physics, but this is field proximity and not a recusal ground.
